title: Replication and Analysis of Ebbinghaus' Forgetting Curve https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4492928/
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 2, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton summarises Murre and Dros's modern replication of Hermann Ebbinghaus's classic forgetting curve, in which a single participant learned and relearned lists of nonsense syllables across retention intervals from 20 minutes to 31 days. The study confirms that the shape of the forgetting curve holds up across language and time period, with rapid initial loss followed by a slower decline. Barton highlights findings on serial position effects (information at the start and end of a learning episode is best retained), a possible role for sleep in consolidating memory around the 24-hour mark, and evidence that implicit memory can persist even when material can no longer be consciously recalled. He draws out classroom applications around spaced repetition, structuring lessons so the most important content sits at the beginning and end, and the value of relearning over pure recall as an assessment method. Because the underlying study used one participant learning nonsense syllables, Barton flags that generalising to real classroom learning needs caution.
points: The forgetting curve highlights the importance of spaced repetition — students retain information better when re-exposed multiple times over a period rather than once.
The serial position effect suggests presenting the most important information at the start and end of a lesson, since that's what's best remembered.
Sleep appears to play a role in memory consolidation, an argument against scheduling high-stakes tests immediately after a break with disrupted sleep.
Savings/relearning scores are consistently higher than recall or recognition scores, so teachers should use varied assessment methods rather than relying on recall alone.
Implicit memory can persist even when students cannot consciously recall material, meaning 'forgotten' content may relearn faster than genuinely new content.
quotes: It is hard to overestimate the importance of Hermann Ebbinghaus' contribution to experimental psychology
The forgetting curve highlights the importance of spaced repetition in learning.
The serial position effect suggests that students are more likely to remember information presented at the beginning and end of a lesson.
The study emphasizes the impact of sleep on memory consolidation.
The research suggests that different types of memory are affected by forgetting in different ways.
The concept of implicit memory indicates that even if students cannot consciously recall information, they may still retain some knowledge of it.
